Lesson 8 · Evaluate the action

Why did some stores adopt alerts themselves?

The randomized pilot supplies one answer. A separate set of 50 stores made its own adoption decisions, and the director wants to understand what their experience adds.

Voluntary adoption · S051–S100 · baseline before week 17

Method in this decision: Selection and causal diagrams

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

Some managers began using alerts in week 17 without being assigned by the pilot. Their stores had different starting conditions from those that continued usual operations. Before calculating an adjusted effect, the analyst reconstructs this selection process. The immediate output is a comparison design: which pre-policy characteristics to use, which population to represent, and how to organize a first like-for-like comparison.

Turn the assignment story into an adjustment strategy

Conditional independence is the working comparison claim

(Y(0), Y(1)) independent of D, conditional on the chosen pre-policy variables X

The claim is that, among stores with the same relevant starting conditions, adoption does not carry further information about the potential outcomes. Positivity adds that both options are represented for the target profiles. Domain knowledge and the collection process supply this argument; a fitted model does not establish it automatically.

Subclassification makes the comparison visible

  • Define strata using pre-policy characteristics.
  • Compare adopters with nonadopters inside each stratum.
  • Calculate one effect estimate per stratum.
  • Weight the stratum estimates for the decision population.

The main example uses two delivery-time groups to expose the arithmetic. It is a first adjustment rather than a claim that delivery grouping captures every starting difference. The next lesson uses location and baseline performance as well.

Put the business history before the model

This study contains S051–S100 only. Delivery time and location are store attributes, and the baseline rate summarizes weeks 1–8. Managers make the adoption decision before week 17. The outcome is the average stockout rate during weeks 17–24.

Ask the managers why they adopted. Stores facing long replenishment cycles or poor prior service have more reason to seek help. Those same starting conditions also predict later stockouts. The diagram records that business logic and makes the comparison question visible.

To estimate the total result of offering alerts, compare stores on factors measured before adoption. A response produced by the policy, such as an emergency order after an alert, belongs in the pathway through which the service works. It should not be silently treated as a starting characteristic.

Read the three basic causal-graph structures

A chain carries part of the policy effect

Earlier review is on the proposed causal pathway. Conditioning on it blocks that pathway, changing a total-effect question into a question about effects not transmitted through review. The intended effect determines whether that is the comparison we want.

A fork creates a backdoor comparison

Delivery conditions can influence adoption and the outcome. Conditioning on the common cause blocks this path. A DAG—directed acyclic graph—expresses an assumed causal structure with arrows and no directed cycles. The arrows represent a business claim about the process, not correlations discovered by software.

A collider can create association when selected

Suppose a store reaches a special review because it adopted the policy or because performance is poor. Restricting analysis to escalated stores links those two reasons for selection. The common consequence is a collider. Conditioning on it, or on information downstream from it, can open a path that was closed.

Follow a path before choosing a control

The three path rules
Structure on the pathWithout conditioningCondition on the middle variable
ChainOpenBlocked
ForkOpenBlocked
ColliderBlockedOpened

A path is blocked when it contains a conditioned non-collider or a collider whose node and descendants are not conditioned on. Two nodes are d-separated when every path between them is blocked. In a larger graph, inspect every path: blocking one backdoor route may leave another open.

Use the backdoor criterion for the total-effect question

  • Start with the intervention and outcome.
  • Find paths entering the intervention through an incoming arrow.
  • Block those non-causal paths with appropriate pre-treatment variables.
  • Keep the intervention’s causal pathways open.

For the standard backdoor adjustment set, avoid descendants of treatment and block each backdoor path. A mediator, collider, and confounder play different roles even if all three predict the outcome. More predictive controls do not necessarily create a better causal comparison.

A proxy carries information without revealing everything

A baseline measure can help represent persistent store conditions. Measurement noise means that a proxy need not remove all confounding. In this case the adoption generator uses measured baseline performance, delivery time, and location; the technical source makes that specific assignment rule inspectable.

Choose a control by its role

Should the analyst adjust for review effort measured after stores receive alerts when estimating the total effect of offering alerts?

Discuss, then reveal

Usually no: review effort is a possible mechanism of the offer’s effect. Use starting conditions to construct the total-effect comparison. A separate mediation question needs a separate target and additional assumptions.

Give each group the weight in the proposed rollout

The director’s proposed offer covers all 50 stores in this cohort. Weight each delivery-group reduction by its share of those 50 stores. This keeps the combined answer aligned with that spending population.

Weight the same target population
GroupTarget weightWithin-group reductionContribution to average
Long lead (4–5 days)36.00%3.311.19
Short lead (2–3 days)64.00%2.061.32

Weighted reduction = sum of the group contributions = 2.51 percentage points

The raw usual-minus-adopter gap was 2.06 points. Grouping on delivery time changes it to 2.51. The calculation shows how starting mix affects the headline comparison.

Delivery groups are an initial simplification. The starting-characteristic table also contains urban location and baseline performance. In the next lesson we use those recorded variables together and show the paired predictions that produce a fuller adjusted estimate.

Give each stratum the weight of the intended population

ATE, ATT, and ATU use different weights

The same stratum comparisons, three population mixes
Delivery stratumReductionAll-store weightAdopter weightNonadopter weight
Long lead (4–5 days)3.310.360.460.25
Short lead (2–3 days)2.060.640.540.75

The ATE weights sum to one across all stores; ATT weights follow the adopter mix; ATU weights follow the nonadopter mix. A different average can therefore result without changing a single within-stratum comparison.

Calculate all three weighted summaries

Using the two delivery strata: all-store estimate 2.51; adopter-weighted estimate 2.64; nonadopter-weighted estimate 2.37 percentage points.

Name these as delivery-stratified estimates. The calculation teaches target weighting; it does not silently add adjustment for location and baseline performance. Matching is one way to make more detailed comparisons when a few broad strata are insufficient.

Use AI to draw an argument that people can inspect

  • Ask domain specialists why each arrow belongs.
  • Separate measured fields from latent causes and proposed mechanisms.
  • Mark the target effect and the proposed adjustment set.
  • Revise the graph when the operating story changes.

Software can draw a DAG and check d-separation implied by the supplied graph. It cannot establish causal direction from a neatly drawn diagram. Precision controls that predict only the outcome can help; variables that explain only treatment may add little outcome information and can worsen overlap.

Write the evaluation design before the final estimate

The design note should identify this cohort, the week-17 adoption date, the weeks 17–24 outcome window, and the target of all 50 stores. Record the pre-policy variables that drove selection and the operational meaning of an alert offer.

This note has a practical role: it stops the statistical target from drifting while models are tried. It also tells the director which evidence belongs to the randomized pilot and which comes from stores choosing the service themselves. Both studies can inform the business, provided their populations and comparisons remain visible.

Update the decision memo

Voluntary adoption requires an explicit selection design. Delivery-group standardization gives a first reduction of 2.51 points for all 50 stores. Use delivery time, location, and prior rate to build the fuller comparison in Lesson 9.

Make the call

Should the analyst adjust for an emergency order placed because the alert told a store to act?

Compare your reasoning

For the total alert-policy effect, keep that response in the policy pathway. Use starting conditions measured before adoption to construct the comparison.

The bigger picture

The most useful control variables come from a story about the order of events. Reconstructing that story connects operations knowledge with the statistical comparison and gives the next estimate a clear target.

After your decision: open the known answer

In this world, voluntary adoption depends on measured delivery time, urban location, and baseline rate. The two delivery groups account for part of that starting mix; the next lesson uses all three recorded characteristics.
